text: Sidney Abbott (July 11, 1937 – April 15, 2015) was an American feminist and lesbian activist and writer. Born on July 11, 1937, into a military family, she described herself as a military brat. She attended Smith College for three years and graduated from the University of New Mexico in 1961. She then pursued graduate studies in urban planning at Columbia University. In 1969, she joined the National Organization for Women (NOW) and became one of the first individuals to advocate for lesbian rights on panels at the New York chapter of NOW and at Columbia University. A member of the Lavender Menace, she co-authored Sappho Was a Right-on Woman: A Liberated View of Lesbianism with Barbara Love in 1971. In the mid-1970s, with Barbara Love, she lobbied for the establishment of a NOW task force focused on lesbian issues, which was eventually created and initially named the "sexuality and lesbian task force"; Abbott co-chaired the task force with a heterosexual woman. At the NOW national conference in Philadelphia in 1976, she successfully demanded that 1% of the organization’s budget be allocated to the task force, a resolution that passed as one of only two to do so. She served on the founding board of the National Gay and Lesbian Task Force and worked to ensure the organization’s board had equal representation of gay men and lesbian women. She was named by the Manhattan Borough President to the community planning board, becoming the first openly gay person to hold that position. She also served as program developer for two departments in the New York City government, co-chaired the New York Performing Arts Center, and was politically active in the North Fork area of Long Island, New York. Abbott and Kate Millett, Phyllis Birkby, Alma Routsong, and Artemis March were among the members of CR One, the first lesbian-feminist consciousness-raising group. She lived in Southold, New York, where in 2007 she founded the Women's Rights are Human Rights nonprofit and in 2008 launched a newsletter, In Our Shoes, covering politics, class, and poverty. Her personal archives are housed in the Sophia Smith Collection at Smith College and in the Radcliff College feminist collection of NOW biographies. Abbott died in a house fire in Southold, New York on April 15, 2015, at the age of 77.
